title: A Learnable France – No car or camera metas

cards.note: Many elements of Germanic architecture are concentrated in Alsace, such as timber framing and half-hip roof. Furthermore, roofs with fish scale tiles are more common in this region. Example
In the older region of Franche-Comté, it is really common to find bell towers with an imperial style dome, along with glazed tiles

In this region, red brick houses are really common.

Example

From Plonkit:

Walls made of uneven cream coloured to orange stones, glued with mortar and often incorporating red brick details can be found in the towns surrounding Paris. Note that the city of Paris itself generally does not have this architecture.

White houses with, often colourful, timber framing are a staple of Basque architecture that extends beyond the Basque speaking area. The timber frame colour (in this case red) will be consistent with other wooden elements, like window shutters and gates.

In and around Toulouse, mainly in old towns, you will commonly find bright orange brick buildings. They differ from brick houses near Belgium by the bricks being brighter, as well as somewhat Mediterranean looking architectural features, such as wooden shutters, being common.

Forests made up entirely of Maritime pines (pinus pinaster) are found in the southwest of the country (Gironde and Landes departments). The whole area will be fairly flat, which is not typical of other areas with such pines.

Example
Alsatian, a dialect of German, is occasionally found in Alsace, a region that changed countries 4 times in modern history. Most bilingual street signs use some variation of gasse or strasse.

Bilingual signs in Basque, a language isolate, are concentrated In the western half of the Pyrénées-Atlantiques department, bordering the Basque speaking regions in Spain. Common letters include K, X and Z. On directional signs, it’s written with a thinner font, which is unique within all minority languages in France.

The word for street is karrika, in contrast to “kalea” in the Spanish Basque country.

From Plonkit:

Breton is a Celtic language, visually most similar to Welsh. Common letters include d, k, w and the letter ñ, which is not found in French. It is commonly found on the Breton peninsula, with bilingual street signs as east as Rennes and rarely Nantes. The Breton word for street is straed.

On the island of Corsica, you may find bilingual signs in Corsican, a Romance language that utilises many features found in Italian, like words almost always ending in vowels. In particular, the endings u/iu/ju, changed from o/io, are common in Corsican. Moreover, placenames will usually have an Italian origin.
In France, phone codes starting with 01 are land lines, located in the region around Paris (Île de France).
The logo of the region Auvergne–Rhône-Alpes is very frequently found near town entry sign in this region. Its blue and white colors with a simple shape makes it easily recognizable.

cards.a: Regional flags and logos – Drapeau catalan
cards.note:
In the southernmost part of mainland France, the département of Pyrénées Orientales often features a variation of the catalan flag, with alternating yellow and red stripes.

Example

The Occitanie region has an easily recognized logo, which also appears on regional bus stops next to the acronym LIO.

Example
Street signs with a red slanted fleur-de-lis are unique to Lille.
Lyon’s street signs feature four corner bolts and an uninterrupted inner white border that cuts a notch for the arrondissement and each bolt.
Montpellier street signs will typically contain a blue ‘M’ on a white background in the top left corner.
Paris uses an iconic green & Prussian blue design with a top arch that has also been replicated in Bucharest, which is sometimes referred to as Paris of the east.
Saint-Étienne has a quite recognizable street sign, with light yellow colored background.
In the region around the cities of Angers and Le Mans, village and city names ending with “-é” are more frequent than in other regions.

In France, village and city names containing the letter W are almost all found in Alsace or in the northern regions that are closer to Belgium.

Usually Alsatian names are recognizable due to the language proximity with German.
The suffix “-rupt” in toponyms is strongly associated with the older region of Lorraine.
In Savoy and sometimes in Jura (along the Switzerland border), toponyms ending with “-oz” or “-az” are common, which is really unfrequent elsewhere.
